title: Installation, the interpreter and your first script

videos.script:
Everything a computer does, somebody wrote down first. {{written}} Not in English, and not in pictures — in a file, in a language the machine can be made to follow. That is all a program is. A file somebody wrote, and a machine that reads it.

This course teaches you to write those files. By the end of it you will have written programs that read a spreadsheet nobody wants to read by hand, that ask a website a question and keep the answer, that do the same tedious thing four thousand times without getting it wrong on the nine hundredth.

{{python}} The language is Python, and the reason is not that it is the easiest — it is that it is the one you are most likely to be asked for. Data work is Python. Automation is Python. The machine learning everybody is talking about is a thin layer of Python over some very fast arithmetic somebody else wrote. Nine other courses here begin where this one ends.

{{first}} Today is the smallest possible amount: getting a Python onto your machine, typing at it, and putting the same lines in a file so they survive you closing the window.

And one thing that is not small at all, which is reading an error. {{traceback}} You are going to see a lot of them. Not because you are bad at this — because everybody who writes Python sees a lot of them, every day, for as long as they do it. The difference between somebody who is learning quickly and somebody who is stuck is almost never talent. It is whether they read the message or panic at the colour of it.

So we are going to break something on purpose, early, and read what the machine says about it. That is the actual skill. Everything else is vocabulary.

I am going to write three lines, make one mistake in them, and read what comes back. Nothing here is staged — I am typing it now.

{{file}} A file called greet.py. Three lines. A name, a greeting built from it, and a print. I save it and I run it — python3 greet.py — and there it is. Hello, Ada.

{{break}} Now the mistake. I am going to spell the name slightly differently on the second line. Not the kind of mistake you notice reading it back; the kind your fingers make. Save. Run.

{{traceback}} And there is the wall of red. Look at the shape of it, because every one of these has the same shape. The last line is the answer. NameError: name 'nmae' is not defined. That is the machine telling you, in plain English, that you used a word it has never been given a meaning for.

{{lines}} Above it, the file and the line number. greet.py, line 2. And above that, the line itself, printed back at you with a little arrow. The machine is showing you exactly where it was standing when it gave up.

{{read}} Read it bottom to top. The bottom line says what went wrong. The line above says where. That is two facts, and between them they locate almost every error you will make this month.

{{fix}} Fix the spelling. Save. Run. Hello, Ada.

Thirty seconds. And the only thing I did was read four words at the bottom of something that looked, for a second, like the computer was angry with me. It is not angry. It is the most literal thing you will ever work with, and that is why it can tell you exactly what it did not understand.

Three things to take out of this lesson.

{{one}} The interpreter is a program that reads your file. You can talk to it directly, at a prompt, and that is good for a question — what does this do, what is in this thing. But a conversation disappears when you close the window. Work goes in a file, and the file is the thing you keep.

{{two}} Running and importing are not the same, and you will meet that properly in lesson seven. For now: python3 followed by a filename runs it, top to bottom, once.

{{three}} And the one that matters most. When it goes wrong, the machine tells you. It tells you what, and it tells you where, and it tells you in that order from the bottom of the message up. Read the last line first. Then the line number. Then look at your file.

{{next}} Next lesson is types — the fact that a value has a kind, and that the kind decides what the operators mean. It is the reason "2" plus "2" can honestly be "22", and why that is not a bug.

Write something today. Something with four lines in it. Break it on purpose and read what comes back.
